title: Use all and any without accepting an empty batch by accident
sources: Python 3.14.8 Built-in Functions: all and any
Python 3.14.8 Built-in Types: Boolean operations and truth-value testing (reviewed 2026-10-03)
masterChecklist: Discrete-math essentials: logic, sets, relations, functions, induction, counting, probability, modular arithmetic
Defensive conditions, validation order, readable Boolean expressions and edge cases
whyItMatters: A validator that says 'every score is valid' may accidentally approve an empty upload. The logic of 'all' and 'any' is correct, but the product's nonempty requirement is a separate condition.
simpleExplanation: `all(test(x) for x in items)` asks whether every item passes. It returns True for an empty iterable because no item fails. `any(test(x) for x in items)` asks whether at least one passes and returns False for an empty iterable. These are the code equivalents of 'for every' and 'there exists.' If a batch must contain at least one item, write that rule explicitly: `bool(items) and all(...)`. Python's `and` short-circuits, so the second part runs only when the first is truthy. For a strict integer score, `type(score) is int` rejects Boolean values, which are subclasses of int.
mentalModel: A teacher says, 'Every paper in this stack is marked.' If the stack is empty, there is no unmarked paper—but the teacher still cannot submit it as a completed class stack. 'Stack is nonempty' is another rule.
outcomes: Add a nonempty precondition to an all-based validator.
Test Boolean and out-of-range scores as invalid domain values.

realWorldExample.scenario: A study-progress importer accepts a batch only when it contains at least one valid score and every score is an integer from 0 to 100.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: Using only all(valid(score) for score in scores) accepts an empty import; using isinstance(score, int) accepts True as score 1.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Validate nonempty input separately, require exact integer type where Boolean is invalid, then check the allowed range and test empty/wrong-type/boundary cases.

explanation: The first two lines show the built-in empty-iterable rules: all is True and any is False.
bool(scores) adds the product rule that an empty batch is not acceptable.
`and` short-circuits: for an empty list, the all expression is not needed.
The generator checks each score lazily; all stops once it finds a failing value.
`type(score) is int` rejects True even though isinstance(True, int) is True.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Replace bool(scores) and with nothing. Predict which invalid input now passes.

procedure: State the domain rule in ordinary language: nonempty, type and range.
Choose all for 'every item' and any for 'at least one item'.
Handle empty input explicitly when the business rule differs from vacuous truth.
Place cheap boundary checks before expensive or unsafe operations.
Test empty, one valid, lower/upper limits, Boolean, wrong type and out-of-range inputs.
For one-pass iterators, do not call bool(iterator) as an emptiness test; choose a deliberate streaming validation strategy.

commonMistakes.why: There is no counterexample in an empty iterable, so all returns True.
commonMistakes.avoid: Add a separate nonempty requirement when the product needs one.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using isinstance(True, int) to enforce a strict score field.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use type(value) is int for this exact-type contract.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using bool(generator) to check whether a generator has items.
commonMistakes.why: A generator object is truthy even when it will yield nothing.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use an explicit bounded peek or materialize only when size is safe.

lab.title: Validate a nonempty score batch
lab.safety: Only fictional in-memory scores are used. Run the exercise in the site's bundled Python worker.
lab.starterCode:
def valid_batch(scores):
    # Require at least one score; all scores must be exact ints in 0..100.
    pass

# Test [], [0, 100], [True], and [101].
guidedSteps: Check the nonempty condition before the all expression.
Require type(score) is int inside the generator.
Test both valid endpoints and three invalid cases.
Explain why all([]) alone would be wrong for this feature.
checks: No external data or files are used.
hints: `bool(scores) and all(...)` expresses two separate rules.
`all` can stop at the first failure.
lab.solutionExplanation: The function first enforces nonempty input and then checks every score. The tests specifically protect the empty-iterable and Boolean-as-integer traps.
challenges: Find the bug: remove bool(scores) from the return expression.
Experiment: pass a generator instead of a list and explain why bool(generator) is not an emptiness test.

simulation.explanation: There is no element that fails the predicate; a nonempty product rule must be added separately.

projectConnection.milestone: Reject empty score batches and enforce exact integer/range rules before writing progress.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: Tests cover empty, valid endpoints, Boolean, wrong type and out-of-range input; no empty import is accepted.

assessment.question: Why does all([]) return True?
assessment.answer: No element in the empty iterable is false.
assessment.explanation: That logical rule is separate from whether an empty batch is useful to the app.

assessment.question: What does any([]) return?
assessment.explanation: There is no element satisfying an existential condition.

assessment.question: Why is bool(generator) not a reliable emptiness check?
assessment.answer: A generator object is truthy even if it yields zero items.
assessment.explanation: One-pass iterators need a deliberate streaming or bounded materialization strategy.
